relationship: Same-chapter regnal framing: Jehoahaz’s accession and succession
rationale: The opening notice names Jehoahaz son of Jehu ruling in Samaria; the closing notice names his death, Samarian burial and succession by Joash, framing this particular king’s account.

relationship: Dynastic conduct parallel: persistence in Jeroboam’s sins
rationale: Jehoahaz follows Jeroboam son of Nebat’s sins without turning away; the earlier assessment gives Jehu the same failure, tracing the stated conduct across the named father and son.

relationship: Prophetic warning and later oppression under Hazael
rationale: Elisha foretells Hazael’s violence toward Israel and his Syrian kingship; the later notice places Israel under Hazael and his son. It does not separately verify every foretold atrocity.

relationship: Same-chapter narrative connection: the Lord hears and shows mercy
rationale: Jehoahaz’s entreaty receives the Lord’s attention to Israel’s affliction; the later notice expressly describes mercy, pity and regard because of the ancestral covenant, without identifying an unnamed intermediary.

relationship: Same-chapter deliverance and reported recovery of Israel’s towns
rationale: The Lord gives Israel deliverance from Syria; the later notice reports Joash recovering Israel’s towns after three victories. This links the stated relief without naming Joash as an expressly identified deliverer in this verse.

relationship: Same-chapter literary repetition: Jeroboam’s sins persist despite relief
rationale: The post-deliverance notice says Israel still does not turn from Jeroboam’s sins; Jehoahaz’s earlier assessment names the same persistence. The grove is an additional detail in the later notice.

relationship: Same-chapter narrative explanation: Syrian destruction and Hazael’s affliction
rationale: The reduced forces are explained by the Syrian king’s destruction; the later summary names Hazael afflicting Israel throughout Jehoahaz’s days, without turning the listed remnant into a total population count.

relationship: Same-chapter regnal framing: Jehoahaz’s acts and opening notice
rationale: The closing formula directs the reader to records of Jehoahaz’s deeds; the opening notice supplies his parentage, Samarian kingship and reign length. The unavailable royal chronicles are not claimed as read.

relationship: Same-chapter succession and accession: Joash son of Jehoahaz
rationale: Jehoahaz’s death notice names Joash succeeding him; the next accession notice expressly identifies Joash son of Jehoahaz ruling Israel in Samaria, keeping him distinct from Judah’s Joash.

relationship: Same-chapter accession and preceding succession: Israel’s Joash
rationale: The accession names Joash son of Jehoahaz in Samaria; the preceding closing notice names Jehoahaz’s burial there and his son Joash’s succession. The synchronism is not independently recalculated.

relationship: Same-chapter regnal assessment parallel: father and son retain Jeroboam’s sins
rationale: Joash’s evil assessment and refusal to turn from Jeroboam’s sins correspond to Jehoahaz’s earlier assessment, connecting these named successive Israelite reigns without importing a new offense.

relationship: Narrative anticipation: Joash’s war with Amaziah
rationale: The closing formula expressly mentions Joash’s acts with Amaziah; the following account narrates their battle, Amaziah’s capture, the breached wall and removed treasures, rather than supplying the unavailable chronicles.

relationship: Repeated royal notice: Joash’s death and Jeroboam’s succession
rationale: Both notices report Joash lying down with his fathers and Jeroboam taking the throne. The later notice adds burial with Israel’s kings, which is not inserted into the earlier sentence.

relationship: Verbal narrative parallel: Israel’s chariot and horseman
rationale: Joash weeps over the dying Elisha and calls him Father and Israel’s chariot and horseman; Elisha used the corresponding cry at Elijah’s departure, with different speakers and circumstances preserved.

relationship: Same-chapter instruction and execution: the bow leads to the eastward shot
rationale: Elisha requests a bow and arrows and they are brought; the later instructions open the east window and command a shot, followed by its stated Syrian-deliverance interpretation.

relationship: Same-chapter narrative sequence: guiding the bow before the commanded shot
rationale: Joash places his hand on the bow and Elisha places his hands on the king’s hands; the next unit records the window instruction and shot, without independently assigning a symbolic meaning to each hand.

relationship: Same-chapter prophetic sign and bounded military outcome against Syria
rationale: The arrow is announced as deliverance against Syria at Aphek; the subsequent rebuke limits Joash to three strikes, and the closing account reports three victories and recovered towns. Total destruction is not asserted as accomplished.

relationship: Same-chapter sign action and rebuke: three ground strikes
rationale: The instruction says Take bows and the king strikes the ground three times before stopping; Elisha’s response explicitly connects that number with three future strikes against Syria, preserving the supplied object wording.

relationship: Same-chapter prophecy and reported outcome: three victories over Syria
rationale: Elisha limits Joash’s victories to three after the stopped ground-striking sign; the later report expressly says Joash struck Hazael’s son three times and recovered towns, without claiming Syria was finished.

relationship: Same-chapter narrative setting: Elisha’s burial and the raider-interrupted funeral
rationale: Elisha’s death, burial and the arrival of Moab’s raiders precede a burial interrupted by a raider, when the body is thrown into Elisha’s grave. The particular grave and threat link the notices.

relationship: Later biblical recollection: Elisha’s posthumous wonders
rationale: The man touches Elisha’s bones, comes to life and stands; Sirach praises Elisha’s body prophesying even in sleep and wonders at his end. The parallel does not add an unreported action by the dead prophet.

relationship: Same-chapter retrospective summary: Hazael’s oppression during Jehoahaz’s reign
rationale: The summary names Hazael afflicting Israel throughout Jehoahaz’s days; the earlier account places Israel in Hazael’s hand and describes the affliction that prompts Jehoahaz’s entreaty.

relationship: Covenantal narrative parallel: Abraham Isaac and Jacob in Israel’s affliction
rationale: Kings attributes the Lord’s mercy to His covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; Exodus names the same three ancestors when God hears Israel’s groaning and remembers His covenant, in a different oppression setting.

relationship: Same-chapter succession and ensuing campaign: Hazael’s son
rationale: Hazael’s death notice names his son, the son of Ader, succeeding him; the next report identifies that son as Joash’s opponent in the recovery of Israel’s towns.

relationship: Same-chapter military outcome and prior prophecy: the three strikes
rationale: Joash strikes Hazael’s son three times and recovers Israel’s towns; Elisha had limited his victories to three. The correspondence concerns the explicit count, without supplying a further campaign or total Syrian destruction.

relationship: Regnal continuity: Amaziah succeeds Judah’s Joash
rationale: The accession identifies Amaziah son of Joash ruling Judah; the earlier death notice names Joash’s burial and his son Amaziah’s succession, keeping Judah’s Joash distinct from the Israelite synchronism.

relationship: Regnal narrative parallel: Amaziah’s age reign and mother
rationale: Both give Amaziah twenty-five years at accession and twenty-nine reigning in Jerusalem, with a Jerusalem mother named Joadin or Joaden. The printed maternal forms remain visible rather than being rewritten.

relationship: Regnal assessment parallel with different qualifications
rationale: Both call Amaziah’s conduct right before the Lord. Kings qualifies it by David and Joash, whereas Chronicles says not with a full heart; those qualifications are retained as different statements.

relationship: Dynastic conduct parallel: upright assessment with high places retained
rationale: Amaziah’s account retains sacrifices and incense at the high places; his father Joash’s account likewise combines an upright assessment with the unremoved high places, supplying the particular earlier comparison.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: the established king punishes his father’s killers
rationale: Both report that when Amaziah’s kingdom was established, he killed the servants who had killed his father, matching the named reprisal without adding a trial procedure.

relationship: Express legal citation: each dies for his own sin
rationale: Kings explicitly grounds sparing the killers’ sons in Moses’ law; Deuteronomy states the corresponding prohibition on fathers dying for children and children for fathers, with each dying for his own sin.

relationship: Historical and legal parallel: the killers’ sons are spared
rationale: Both say Amaziah did not kill the servants’ sons and quote the prohibition on intergenerational execution. The quoted legal basis is retained without turning this account into an independent legal adjudication.

relationship: Military narrative parallel with distinct places and outcomes retained
rationale: Kings reports ten thousand Edomites struck at Gaimela and the Rock captured and renamed; Chronicles reports ten thousand of Seir’s sons struck in the Valley of Salts and adds captives thrown from a cliff. The places and actions are not equated.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: Amaziah challenges Israel’s Joash
rationale: Both have Amaziah send Israel’s Joash a face-to-face challenge, with Jehu in the stated ancestry. Jehoahaz and Joachaz remain the supplied parental forms rather than an independently reconstructed genealogy.

relationship: Literary narrative parallel: the Lebanon plant-and-marriage fable
rationale: Both replies tell of a lesser plant requesting the cedar’s daughter for its son and being trampled by animals. Kings says thornbush and Chronicles achouch; no independent translation of achouch is supplied.

relationship: Historical speech parallel: Idumean victory and the warning to stay home
rationale: Both replies connect Amaziah’s lifted heart with victory over Idumea, tell him to remain home and warn that he and Judah will fall. The speech is not changed into an independent diagnosis of his motives.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: the refused warning leads to Baithsamys
rationale: Both say Amaziah did not listen and describe the kings facing one another at Baithsamys in Judah. Chronicles adds a divine-purpose explanation, retained as its additional statement.

relationship: Battle narrative parallel: Judah’s defeat and flight
rationale: Kings says Judah stumbled before Israel and each fled to his dwelling; Chronicles reports Judah routed and each fleeing to his tent. The corresponding defeat is retained with the different dwelling terms.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: Amaziah captured and Jerusalem’s wall breached
rationale: Both name Joash capturing Amaziah at Baithsamys and four hundred cubits of Jerusalem’s wall torn down between the Ephraim and Corner gates. No further wall measurement or reconstruction is inferred.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: treasures removed and return to Samaria
rationale: Both report gold, silver, temple articles, royal treasures and a group described by mixed terminology taken before the return to Samaria. Chronicles adds Abdedom; neither group is independently recast as hostages.

relationship: Repeated royal notice: Joash’s acts and war with Amaziah
rationale: Both closing notices specifically refer Joash’s deeds and his encounter with Amaziah to Israel’s royal chronicles. This matches the repeated named-war notice without claiming those unavailable records were read.

relationship: Repeated royal notice: Joash’s death and Jeroboam’s throne
rationale: Both report Joash lying down with his fathers and Jeroboam succeeding. This verse adds burial in Samaria with Israel’s kings, preserving that fuller description without inserting it into the earlier notice.

relationship: Regnal narrative parallel: Amaziah’s fifteen years after Joash
rationale: Both say Amaziah lived fifteen years after the death of Israel’s Joash. Kings names Joash’s father Jehoahaz and Chronicles Joachaz, retaining their stated forms without recalculating accession dates.

relationship: Royal-record formula parallel: Amaziah’s remaining deeds
rationale: Both closing formulas refer Amaziah’s other acts to royal records; Kings names Judah’s chronicles and Chronicles the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel. The record titles remain distinct and are not claimed as read.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: conspiracy flight and death at Lachish
rationale: Both describe an attack against Amaziah, his flight to Lachish or Lachis and pursuers killing him there. Chronicles adds his departure from the Lord; the place forms and added explanation remain separate.

relationship: Burial narrative parallel: Amaziah carried on horses
rationale: Both report Amaziah carried on horses and buried with his fathers in David’s city; Kings additionally names Jerusalem. The particular transport and burial link the notices without adding a funeral procession.

relationship: Regnal narrative parallel with preserved royal name forms
rationale: Both describe the people making Amaziah’s sixteen-year-old son king in his place. Kings names Azariah and Chronicles Uzziah; the matching succession framework does not rewrite either supplied name.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel with preserved place forms: Ailoth and Ailath
rationale: Kings reports Ailoth built and restored to Judah after the king lay down with his fathers; Chronicles reports Ailath built and restored after the king’s death, retaining the distinct place forms and unnamed king wording.

relationship: Same-chapter succession and accession: Jeroboam son of Joash
rationale: The accession explicitly names Jeroboam son of Joash ruling in Samaria; the preceding death notice had named him succeeding Joash, linking the same named succession without identifying him with Jeroboam son of Nebat.

relationship: Dynastic conduct parallel: Joash and Jeroboam retain the earlier Jeroboam’s sins
rationale: Jeroboam son of Joash is assessed as persisting in Jeroboam son of Nebat’s sins; his father Joash receives the corresponding assessment, preserving the distinction between the two Jeroboams.

relationship: Prophetic name-and-parentage connection: Jonah son of Amathi or Amittai
rationale: Kings names Jonah son of Amathi as the prophet of the boundary oracle; Jonah opens with the Lord’s word to Jonah son of Amittai. The matching prophetic designation does not insert the boundary oracle into Jonah’s Nineveh commission.

relationship: Narrative parallel: the Lord sees Israel’s affliction
rationale: The Lord sees Israel’s bitter humiliation and lack of help; the earlier notice says He sees Israel’s Syrian affliction and listens to Jehoahaz. The different reigns and the later description’s added details remain distinct.

relationship: Covenantal mercy parallel: Israel is spared destruction
rationale: The Lord has not spoken of blotting out Israel’s seed and saves them through Jeroboam; the earlier notice says His ancestral covenant restrains destruction and expulsion. Mercy is linked without making Jeroboam’s conduct righteous.

relationship: Same-chapter royal closing notice and the preceding boundary report
rationale: The closing formula names Jeroboam’s warfare and restoration of Damascus and Aimath to Judah in Israel; the earlier notice reports Israel’s shifted boundary from Aimath’s entrance. The distinct geographical and Judah wording is preserved rather than harmonized.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated succession wording: Azariah son of Amaziah
rationale: This closing notice names Azariah son of Amaziah reigning in his father’s place, as the earlier notice does. Its placement after Jeroboam’s death is retained; Zechariah is not substituted as its stated successor.

relationship: Regnal continuity: Azariah son of Amaziah
rationale: Both notices identify Azariah succeeding his father Amaziah in Judah; the accession adds the Jeroboam synchronism, while the earlier notice states the people’s action and the son’s age.

relationship: Regnal narrative parallel with preserved royal name forms and figures
rationale: Both give sixteen at accession, fifty-two years in Jerusalem and a Jerusalem mother named Chalia. Kings names Azariah and Chronicles Uzziah, retaining those forms without independently adjusting the figures.

relationship: Regnal conduct parallel: the Amaziah comparison
rationale: Both assess the king’s conduct as right before the Lord according to his father Amaziah. The comparison is retained within the Azariah and Uzziah notices without importing Chronicles’ later sanctuary episode here.

relationship: Dynastic conduct parallel: high places remain under father and son
rationale: Azariah’s notice says the high places remained with continuing sacrifices and incense; Amaziah’s earlier notice makes the corresponding qualification, connecting the stated father-and-son conduct without asserting identical entire reigns.

relationship: Narrative parallel: lasting leprosy and Jotham’s administration
rationale: Both report leprosy lasting until death, an Apphousoth or apphousoth house, and Jotham judging the people. Kings says the king reigned in that house, while Chronicles says he lived there; Chronicles also adds the sanctuary confrontation and forehead outbreak.

relationship: Royal closing notices with distinct record attributions
rationale: Kings directs Azariah’s remaining acts to Judah’s royal chronicles; Chronicles attributes Uzziah’s acts to Jessias the prophet. These are parallel closing notices, without equating the records or renaming the supplied prophet.

relationship: Regnal narrative parallel: the king’s death and Jotham’s succession
rationale: Both close the Azariah or Uzziah account with death, burial and son Jotham’s succession. Chronicles specifies the field of the kings’ burial because of leprosy; the burial descriptions are retained without harmonization.

relationship: Same-chapter dynastic narrative connection: Zechariah and Jehu’s fourth-generation promise
rationale: Zechariah is introduced as Jeroboam’s son ruling Israel; the later comment explicitly recalls the Lord’s promise of Jehu’s sons on the throne to the fourth generation. No additional regnal calculation is supplied.

relationship: Dynastic conduct parallel: Zechariah and his father Jeroboam
rationale: Zechariah’s notice retains Jeroboam son of Nebat’s sins, as his father Jeroboam son of Joash’s assessment had done. The earlier and later Jeroboams remain distinct named figures.

relationship: Same-chapter conspiracy outcome and ensuing reign: Sellum in Samaria
rationale: Sellum son of Jabis and Keblaam are named in the conspiracy against Zechariah, after which Sellum reigns; the later notice gives Sellum’s one-month Samarian reign. Keblaam is not independently turned into a place.

relationship: Same-chapter royal closing notice and Zechariah’s narrated reign
rationale: Zechariah’s closing formula points to the royal chronicles; his opening and death notices supply the six-month reign and named conspiracy. This particular reign is linked without claiming the chronicles were consulted.

relationship: Explicit retrospective prophecy: Jehu’s fourth-generation throne promise
rationale: The narrator recalls the Lord’s promise that Jehu’s sons would sit on Israel’s throne to the fourth generation and says it happened; the earlier oracle records that promise in its own setting.

relationship: Same-chapter accession and prior conspiracy: Sellum succeeds Zechariah
rationale: The accession gives Sellum son of Jabis a month in Samaria; the preceding account names him after Zechariah’s killing as king in his place. The short reign does not erase Keblaam from that earlier conspiracy.

relationship: Same-chapter narrative succession: Manaem kills Sellum and becomes king
rationale: Manaem son of Gaddi kills Sellum in Samaria; the later accession names the same Manaem ruling Israel for ten years. Tharsila and the later Thersa wording are not independently equated.

relationship: Same-chapter royal closing notice recalls Sellum’s conspiracy
rationale: The closing formula expressly mentions Sellum’s conspiracy; the earlier notice names his and Keblaam’s conspiracy against Zechariah and the resulting succession. The unavailable chronicles receive no claim of having been read.

relationship: Same-chapter narrative connection: Manaem’s violence after the Samarian coup
rationale: The Thersa assault is attributed to Manaem after the account of his killing Sellum in Samaria. The link retains the named actor and sequence without equating Thersa and Tharsila or relocating the recorded atrocity.

relationship: Same-chapter regnal framing: Manaem and his son Phakeias
rationale: The opening gives Manaem son of Gaddi ten years in Samaria; the closing reports his death and son Phakeias’s succession, framing this named king’s reign without recalculating the synchronism.

relationship: Same-chapter dynastic conduct parallel: Manaem and Phakeias
rationale: Manaem and his son Phakeias are each assessed as evil and not turning from Jeroboam son of Nebat’s sins. Their parallel conduct does not merge their reigns or their other acts.

relationship: Same-chapter payment and collection: silver given to Phul
rationale: Manaem gives Phul a thousand talents of silver for support; the next notice describes silver exacted from Israel’s mighty men and the Assyrian king’s departure, without an independent currency or population calculation.

relationship: Same-chapter collection and preceding payment to the Assyrian king
rationale: The levy of fifty shekels per mighty man is connected to giving silver to Assyria’s king; the preceding notice names Phul and the thousand talents. The figures are preserved without calculating a contributor census.

relationship: Same-chapter royal closing notice and Manaem’s narrated silver payment
rationale: Manaem’s closing formula refers his remaining deeds to the royal chronicles; the preceding account supplies his payment to Phul and the levy on Israel. This connects specific narrated acts without claiming access to the chronicles.

relationship: Same-chapter succession and accession: Phakeias son of Manaem
rationale: Manaem’s closing notice names his son Phakeias succeeding him; the next notice gives Phakeias son of Manaem a two-year Samarian reign, matching the named son while preserving the supplied spelling.

relationship: Same-chapter accession and prior succession: Phakeias
rationale: The accession explicitly names Phakeias son of Manaem over Israel in Samaria; the preceding death notice reports Manaem’s son Phakeias becoming king in his place, without an independently derived calendar.

relationship: Same-chapter dynastic conduct parallel: the father’s and son’s Jeroboam assessment
rationale: Phakeias’s evil conduct and persistence in Jeroboam’s sins correspond to Manaem’s earlier assessment, linking these named successive reigns without assigning their separate conspiracies to one another.

relationship: Same-chapter conspiracy outcome and accession: Phakee son of Romelias
rationale: Phakee son of Romelias, the third-ranking officer, kills Phakeias and succeeds him; the later accession names Phakee ruling Israel. The fifty men from the four hundred remain as stated rather than being independently identified.

relationship: Same-chapter royal closing notice and Phakeias’s narrated reign
rationale: The closing formula names Phakeias’s remaining deeds; his preceding notices give his accession, conduct and death in Phakee’s conspiracy. The linked narrative does not claim the royal chronicles were read.

relationship: Same-chapter accession and preceding coup: Phakee son of Romelias
rationale: The accession names Phakee son of Romelias ruling Israel; the preceding account identifies him as the officer who killed Phakeias and became king, preserving the two similar royal names as different people.

relationship: Same-chapter regnal assessment parallel across the coup: Jeroboam’s sins persist
rationale: Phakee’s assessment retains the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, as Phakeias’s earlier assessment did. The repeated conduct spans the change of king without implying a father-and-son relationship.

relationship: Historical deportation parallel: northern places and the later Samarian capture
rationale: The Assyrian king deports named northern regions in Phakee’s days; the later capture of Samaria likewise ends in deportation to Assyria. The different reigns, campaigns and listed destinations are not collapsed into one event.

relationship: Succession and later accession notice: Hoshea son of Ela
rationale: The conspiracy account names Hoshea son of Ela killing Phakee and succeeding him; the later accession identifies Hoshea in Samaria. The twentieth-year Jotham and twelfth-year Ahaz statements are preserved without an independent chronology solution.

relationship: Same-chapter royal closing notice and Phakee’s narrated reign
rationale: The closing formula names Phakee’s remaining deeds; the preceding notices recount his reign, the Assyrian deportation and Hoshea’s conspiracy. The particular royal account is linked without claiming the chronicles were consulted.

relationship: Same-chapter accession and earlier succession: Jotham son of Azariah
rationale: Jotham’s accession names his father Azariah; the earlier death notice names Azariah’s son Jotham succeeding him. The Phakee synchronism is retained rather than independently recalculated.

relationship: Regnal narrative parallel: Jotham’s age reign and mother
rationale: Both give Jotham twenty-five at accession and sixteen years in Jerusalem, naming his mother Jerusa or Jerousa daughter of Sadok. The different maternal forms remain visible without a new chronology claim.

relationship: Regnal conduct parallel with preserved paternal forms
rationale: Both call Jotham’s conduct right according to his father; Kings names Ozias and Chronicles Uzziah. Chronicles adds the sanctuary exception and people’s corruption, retaining those details in its own account.

relationship: Construction narrative parallel: the Upper Gate of the Lord’s house
rationale: Both attribute the Upper Gate’s construction to Jotham; Chronicles adds work on Ophla’s wall. Kings’ qualification about continued high-place sacrifices remains distinct from that construction notice.

relationship: Royal-record formula parallel: Jotham’s remaining deeds
rationale: Both refer Jotham’s remaining acts to royal records; Kings names Judah’s chronicles and Chronicles the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel, also mentioning war. The titles and added detail remain distinct.

relationship: Narrative anticipation: Raasson and Phakee attack Judah
rationale: The Lord begins sending Raasson of Syria and Phakee son of Romelias against Judah; the following reign account names those same kings besieging Ahaz at Jerusalem, without making the two notices identical in scope.

relationship: Regnal narrative parallel: Jotham’s burial and Ahaz’s succession
rationale: Both report Jotham’s death, burial in David’s city and succession by his son Ahaz, matching the named royal transition without adding a different burial place or regnal year.

relationship: Accession and preceding succession: Ahaz son of Jotham
rationale: Ahaz’s accession names him as Jotham’s son ruling Judah; Jotham’s death notice had named Ahaz succeeding him, linking the explicit transition without reconciling the synchronisms of neighboring reigns.

relationship: Regnal narrative parallel: Ahaz’s age reign and David comparison
rationale: Both give Ahaz twenty years at accession, sixteen years in Jerusalem and failure to do right as David had done. The comparison does not turn Ahaz into David’s immediate biological son.

relationship: Regnal conduct parallel with different child and way descriptions
rationale: Kings names Jeroboam’s way and Ahaz’s son passing through fire; Chronicles names Israel’s kings, idols and children passing through fire. The singular and plural, place detail and descriptions remain as supplied.

relationship: Worship-practice parallel: incense beneath leafy trees
rationale: Both describe Ahaz burning incense at high places and beneath leafy trees. Kings also names hills and sacrifices, while Chronicles names rooftops; the different locations and actions are not silently combined.

relationship: Military narrative and earlier notice: Raasson and Phakee against Judah
rationale: Raasson and Phakee besiege Ahaz at Jerusalem but do not succeed in the stated battle; the earlier notice names the Lord beginning to send these kings against Judah, without transferring a different campaign’s casualties here.

relationship: Historical place parallel with reversed control and retained forms
rationale: The earlier reign account reports Ailoth restored to Judah; this notice has Raasson restore Ailath to Syria and expel Judeans, with Idumeans settling there. The place forms and distinct Syrian and Idumean actors remain explicit.

relationship: Historical request parallel: Ahaz seeks Assyrian help
rationale: Both have Ahaz send to Assyria’s king for help; Kings supplies his slave-and-son address and names the Syrian and Israelite threats. The later outcomes in the two accounts are not equated.

relationship: Historical payment parallel with a different reported result
rationale: Both describe Ahaz taking goods from the Lord’s and king’s houses and giving to Assyria’s king. Chronicles adds rulers’ goods and says it brought no help; Kings’ subsequent Damascus capture remains its own report.

relationship: Same-chapter request and reported response: Assyria attacks Damascus
rationale: Ahaz asks Assyria’s king to save him from Syria and Israel; the later notice expressly says the king listens and captures Damascus, deports it and kills Raasson. It does not assert an additional conquest of Israel here.

relationship: Same-chapter design and reported construction: the Damascus altar
rationale: Ahaz sends Uriah the Damascus altar’s likeness and full design; the next notice says Uriah builds according to what the king sent. No unreported material, dimension or motive is supplied.

relationship: Same-chapter construction and preceding design: Uriah’s altar
rationale: Uriah builds according to everything Ahaz sent from Damascus; the preceding notice identifies the seen altar, its likeness and construction design sent to the priest, grounding the particular commission.

relationship: Same-chapter narrative sequence: the king approaches the altar and offers
rationale: The king sees the altar and goes up onto it; the following unit lists his burnt offering, sacrifice, drink offering and peace-offering blood. The first notice is not expanded with an unreported consecration ceremony.

relationship: Same-chapter royal offering and ensuing instructions for the great altar
rationale: Ahaz’s own offerings and blood application are followed by his detailed commands for king and people’s offerings on the great altar. The performed acts and later prescribed acts remain distinct.

relationship: Same-chapter arrangement and later assignment: the bronze altar
rationale: Ahaz moves the bronze altar to the other altar’s north side; the next instruction assigns offerings to the great altar and says the bronze altar is for him for the morning. The morning wording is not replaced with inquiry.

relationship: Same-chapter command and compliance: Uriah performs Ahaz’s instructions
rationale: Ahaz specifies the offerings on the great altar and reserves the bronze altar for himself for the morning; the following notice says Uriah did everything commanded, without independently changing that reservation’s wording.

relationship: Same-chapter compliance and preceding command: the two altars
rationale: The narrator says Uriah did all Ahaz commanded; the preceding command supplies the offerings for the great altar and the bronze altar’s stated morning reservation, keeping obedience to the king distinct from divine approval.

relationship: Temple-object continuity: the Sea and its bronze oxen
rationale: Ahaz takes the Sea off its bronze oxen and places it on stone; the construction account describes twelve cattle beneath the Sea, with the Sea above them. The particular earlier arrangement is linked without independently translating mechonoth or adding a destruction of the oxen.

relationship: Same-chapter narrative context: temple alterations and the Assyrian king
rationale: The entrance alteration is expressly because of Assyria’s king; the earlier notices narrate Ahaz’s appeal, gifts, the Damascus capture and meeting that king. The link does not independently explain the seat’s foundation or the king’s private motive.

relationship: Royal-record formula parallel: Ahaz’s remaining deeds
rationale: Both refer Ahaz’s remaining acts to royal records; Kings names Judah’s chronicles and Chronicles the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel. Their titles remain distinct and the cited books are not claimed as read.

relationship: Regnal narrative parallel: Ahaz’s death and Hezekiah’s succession
rationale: Both report Ahaz’s death, burial in David’s city and succession by his son Hezekiah. Chronicles adds exclusion from the kings’ tombs, which is preserved without adding that qualification to Kings.

relationship: Accession and earlier succession: Hoshea son of Ela
rationale: Hoshea’s accession in Samaria names the same son of Ela who killed Phakee and became king in his place. The twelfth-year Ahaz and twentieth-year Jotham statements remain as supplied without chronological harmonization.

relationship: Regnal conduct comparison: Hoshea and his predecessor
rationale: Hoshea is called evil, with an explicit qualification that he was not like earlier Israelite kings; Phakee’s preceding assessment names evil and Jeroboam’s sins. The qualification is retained without assigning an unstated comparative degree.

relationship: Same-chapter narrative contrast: paid manaa and the withheld payment
rationale: Hoshea becomes the Assyrian king’s slave and pays manaa; the next notice says he did not bring manaa that year and sent to Egypt. Manaa is retained without independently translating it or establishing a regular annual rate.

relationship: Same-chapter narrative reversal: the vassal payment gives way to imprisonment
rationale: The king finds wrongdoing after Hoshea’s Egyptian messengers and withheld manaa, then besieges and imprisons him; the preceding notice records his enslavement and payment. Segor’s identity is not independently substituted from another edition.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: Samaria’s three-year siege
rationale: This siege notice gives three years, and its immediately following capture notice connects the siege to Samaria’s capture. The later account likewise describes the siege and capture after three years, adding Hezekiah and Hoshea synchronisms without inserting them into this notice.

relationship: Historical deportation parallel with preserved place descriptions
rationale: Both place Samaria’s capture in Hoshea’s ninth year and report deportation to Assyria with Alae, Abor, Gozan and Ore of the Medes. The different river descriptions remain as printed without a geographical reconstruction.

relationship: Covenantal contrast: the Exodus God and worship of other gods
rationale: Kings attributes Israel’s fall to sin against the Lord who brought them out of Egypt and to fearing other gods; the commandments name that deliverance and forbid other gods, images and bowing to them.

relationship: Covenantal contrast: adopting the displaced nations’ practices
rationale: Kings says Israel followed the nations’ ordinances; Deuteronomy forbids learning their abominations and describes their removal because of such practices. The law’s particular examples are not inserted into this incomplete-running sentence.

relationship: Same-chapter narrative expansion: the high places and their practices
rationale: The accusation names high places throughout Israel’s cities; the next units describe pillars, groves and incense at those high places. The surrounding continuation supplies particular practices without independently rewriting the clothed-in-words clause.

relationship: Covenantal contrast: hills trees pillars and groves
rationale: Kings describes pillars and groves on high hills and beneath leafy trees; Deuteronomy directs destruction of the nations’ worship sites on mountains, hills and beneath trees, along with pillars and groves.

relationship: Same-chapter narrative continuity: the sites of the condemned incense
rationale: The incense accusation refers to all those high places; the preceding unit locates the pillars and groves on high hills and under leafy trees. The associates-and-engraving wording remains intact without an independent paraphrase.

relationship: Command and contrary practice: serving idols
rationale: Kings says Israel served idols despite the Lord’s prohibition; the commandments forbid other gods, making images and bowing to or serving them. This matches the explicit forbidden worship rather than an independently identified idol.

relationship: Prophetic summons parallel: servants call for turning from evil
rationale: Kings summarizes the Lord’s prophets calling Israel and Judah to turn from evil and keep His commands; the Jeremiah passage likewise uses the language of sending prophetic servants with the summons to turn. The connection does not identify every prophet in Kings.

relationship: Same-chapter warning and refusal: the prophetic appeal is not heard
rationale: After the Lord warns through prophets to turn and keep His law, the people do not listen and harden their back. The response is connected to that particular appeal without replacing the supplied back imagery.

relationship: Verbal prophetic parallel: following vanity and becoming vain
rationale: Kings says the people followed vain things and became vain; Jeremiah asks why the fathers withdrew, followed futile things and became futile. The shared pursuit-and-result wording is retained without identifying a single historical audience.

relationship: Thematic and verbal parallel: futile thought and exchanged worship
rationale: Kings connects abandoned testimony, vanity and imitation of nations; Romans describes people becoming futile in thought and exchanging God’s glory for images. The parallel does not make Paul explicitly cite this Kings passage.

relationship: Narrative retrospective connection: Israel’s two heifers
rationale: The summary names a casting of two heifers among Israel’s abandoned-commandment practices; the earlier Jeroboam account explicitly makes two golden heifers and places them at Bethel and Dan, while the summary also names other worship.

relationship: Covenantal contrast: cast images and worship of the heavenly host
rationale: Kings lists cast heifers, groves, bowing to heaven’s host and serving Baal; the commandment forbids images of heavenly and earthly things and serving them. The distinct listed objects are retained rather than reduced to one idol.

relationship: Covenantal contrast: children through fire divination and omens
rationale: Kings lists sons and daughters led through fire, divinations and omens; Deuteronomy expressly forbids child purification by fire, divination and omens among the nations’ abominations. The acts are compared without independently resolving their ritual details.

relationship: Narrative comparison across the kingdoms: a child through fire
rationale: The summary charges Israel with leading sons and daughters through fire; Judah’s Ahaz had been reported leading his son through fire according to the nations’ abominations. The singular and plural and the different royal settings remain distinct.

relationship: Same-chapter theological explanation and preceding deportation: Israel removed
rationale: The narrator says the Lord’s anger removed Israel from His presence; the earlier notice reports Samaria captured and Israel deported. Judah alone remaining is preserved without extending it into a claim about every individual Israelite.

relationship: Narrative assessment: Judah follows condemned Israelite practices
rationale: The summary says Judah also disobeyed and followed Israel’s ordinances; Ahaz’s account names Jeroboam’s way, the child through fire and high-place worship. That particular Judah example does not claim every king acted identically.

relationship: Same-chapter narrative explanation: rejected testimony and expulsion
rationale: The verse first says they rejected the Lord throughout Israel’s seed, then describes His giving them to plunderers and casting them out. The earlier accusation of abandoned testimony supplies the human refusal without reversing the sentence’s agents.

relationship: Historical retrospective reference: Israel’s separation and Jeroboam’s kingship
rationale: Kings recalls Israel apart from David’s house and making Jeroboam son of Nebat king; the earlier account reports the separation and the installation of a king named Jeroboam over Israel. The named dynastic break is linked without adding the parentage to the shorter target.

relationship: Historical retrospective assessment: persistence in Jeroboam’s sin
rationale: The summary says Israel continued every sin Jeroboam committed; the earlier account narrates his two golden heifers and calls the matter a sin. This particular example does not replace the summary’s broader every-sin wording.

relationship: Historical and covenantal parallel: deportation after disobedience
rationale: Both connect Assyrian deportation with refusal of the Lord’s covenant and commands; this summary additionally names the prophetic warnings and continuing exile. The later account’s destination list remains its own detail.

relationship: Covenant warning and later exile: removal from the inherited land
rationale: Kings reports Israel removed from the Lord’s presence and deported from its land; Deuteronomy warns of removal from the inherited land and scattering among nations. The broader warning is not reduced to only this deportation.

relationship: Same-chapter resettlement and ensuing worship notices: nations in Samaria
rationale: The king settles people from the named places in Samaria’s cities instead of Israel; the later notices describe each nation’s gods there. The supplied Chountha and Chouth forms are retained without a reconstructed migration census.

relationship: Same-chapter event and reported explanation: lions among the settlers
rationale: The narrator says the Lord sends lions that kill some settlers; their report to Assyria’s king repeats the lions and attributes them to ignorance of the land’s God, preserving the report as the settlers’ explanation.

relationship: Same-chapter reported crisis and preceding narrative: the deadly lions
rationale: The settlers tell Assyria’s king that lions are killing them and give their explanation; the earlier narrative records lack of fear of the Lord and lions killing some. The report is distinguished from an independent ritual diagnosis.

relationship: Same-chapter command and reported response: instruction in the land’s God
rationale: The king commands people to go and live there and instruct them about the land’s God; the next notice reports one deported priest living in Bethel and teaching how to fear the Lord. The command’s unspecific plural wording is not rewritten into a supplied singular.

relationship: Same-chapter reported instruction and preceding royal command
rationale: A returned priest resides at Bethel and enlightens the settlers about fearing the Lord; the prior command had called for residents to instruct them about the land’s God, without expressly naming Bethel in the command.

relationship: Same-chapter general statement and named examples: the nations’ own gods
rationale: The general notice says each nation makes its own gods and places them in high-place houses; the following list names particular peoples and gods. The names remain as supplied without independent identifications of the deities.

relationship: Same-chapter named examples and preceding pattern: Babylon Chouth and Aimath
rationale: The gods of Babylon, Chouth and Aimath instantiate the preceding statement that each nation made its own gods. Sokchothbainith, Nerigel and Asimath remain supplied names without additional mythological descriptions.

relationship: Same-chapter narrative comparison: children burned for named gods
rationale: The settlers’ notice names the Evites’ gods and Seppharouain’s sons burned for Adramelech and Anemelech; the earlier Israelite summary had condemned children through fire. The peoples, named recipients and different actions remain distinct.

relationship: Same-chapter literary continuation: fearing the Lord alongside their own worship
rationale: The verse twice says they feared the Lord while describing high-place abominations, priests and rites; the next notice explicitly joins fear of the Lord with serving their own gods, preserving both assertions without making the worship exclusive.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated assessment: fear of the Lord with service of other gods
rationale: Both notices say these nations fear the Lord while serving their own gods or carved images. The final notice extends that pattern to sons and grandsons, without changing the repeated fear clause into its opposite.

relationship: Express retrospective naming reference: Jacob called Israel
rationale: The verse identifies the commanded people as Jacob’s sons and recalls his naming as Israel; Genesis records Jacob’s name question and the declaration of Israel as his name. The affirmative they-fear wording in Kings remains unchanged.

relationship: Covenantal prohibition parallel: no other gods bowing or service
rationale: The covenant command forbids fearing, bowing to, serving and sacrificing to other gods; the commandments likewise exclude other gods and forbid bowing to or serving images. The sacrifice clause remains a Kings detail.

relationship: Covenantal deliverance and exclusive allegiance: the Lord brought Israel out
rationale: Kings commands fear, worship and sacrifice to the Lord who brought Israel from Egypt with strength and raised arm; the commandments name that same deliverance before forbidding other gods, retaining Kings’ additional action language.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated covenant charge: keep the written commandments
rationale: The covenant quotation commands continued performance of written ordinances, judgments, law and commandments; the earlier prophetic summary calls for keeping the Lord’s commandments, ordinances and law. The two distinct stated forms of warning remain visible.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated covenant prohibition: no fear of other gods
rationale: The command not to forget the covenant repeats the prohibition on fearing other gods already given when the covenant is introduced. It preserves the quoted obligation rather than asserting the settlers performed it.

relationship: Same-chapter exclusive allegiance and promised rescue: fear the Lord
rationale: The command to fear the Lord with promised rescue from enemies continues the earlier command to fear Him alone because He brought Israel out of Egypt. The promise is not changed into a narrated rescue of these settlers.

relationship: Same-chapter closing instruction within the covenant quotation
rationale: You shall not listen to their judgment closes the preceding commands about fearing the Lord and refusing other gods. The supplied wording remains an instruction, rather than being replaced with a past-tense report that they did not listen.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated assessment and continuation through descendants
rationale: The final notice repeats fear of the Lord alongside service to carved images, then extends the fathers’ practice to sons and grandsons. The repeated mixed practice is retained without claiming exclusive fidelity to the covenant.
